video_title: Checking back in with Greenlight America
gist: Greenlight America CEO Matt Traldy tells David Roberts (live at a Canary Media Climate Week NYC event) that safe-harbored wind/solar must clear local permitting by early-to-mid 2028 to capture credits, driving an explosion of county hearings where organized local supporters lift Greenlight's win rate to 79%. He expects only a modest 20-30% post-deadline dip, flags restrictive ordinances and blue-state storage bans, and warns that data center backlash is already pushing would-be supporters away from clean energy. Note: the transcript repeats the intro, figures differ between intro and interview (55.7 vs 67 GW; staff counts), and it cuts off mid-Q&A.

themes.theme: Tax-credit deadline sprint and post-2028 outlook

insights.claim: Under last year's reconciliation bill (OBBBA), wind and solar tax credits are being phased out while credits for many other clean technologies were left in place.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Policy risk is technology-specific: wind/solar face a cliff while other clean tech keeps credit support.
insights.quote: It did phase out tax credits for wind and solar specifically. It left in place tax credits for many other technologies

insights.claim: Large developers Greenlight works with report having started construction (often via offsite equipment purchases, per IRS rules) on virtually all projects already in advanced planning, meeting the July start-of-construction deadline.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: A large safe-harbored pipeline exists on paper; the binding constraint has shifted to permitting and on-site build.
insights.quote: we hear that they've started construction on virtually all of their projects that are already in advanced planning

insights.claim: Because projects that began construction in 2025 must be placed in service within four years (by end-2029), and on-site build plus interconnection takes 12-18 months minimum, developers must clear local permitting and break ground by early-to-mid 2028.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Expect a surge of local permitting hearings through 2027-early 2028; local approvals become the critical path for credit capture.
insights.quote: they'll have to be through the permitting phase and be able to start building on the ground by early to mid 2028

insights.claim: Citing Wood Mackenzie, roughly 216-240 GW of solar and about 20-plus GW of wind have been safe harbored, versus a historical good year of about 50 GW of build.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: The safe-harbored backlog equals several years of prior US build pace, implying a multi-year deployment wave if permits clear.
insights.quote: something like 216 to 240 gawatts of solar and another maybe 20ome gigawatts of wind has been safe harbored

insights.claim: Industry contacts expect only a modest, temporary post-deadline dip in deployment, with the largest estimate heard being a 20-30% decline for a year or two, cushioned by rising power demand.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Downside to post-2028 solar/wind volumes may be smaller than feared; load growth supports continued demand.
insights.quote: the largest number we've heard on that front for folks who've been willing to put a number on is maybe 20 to 30% of a decline

insights.claim: Traldy says he is not worried about the US being overbuilt with clean energy after the sprint.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Counter to the pull-forward-then-bust narrative; the speaker sees structural demand outstripping supply.
insights.quote: Uh I'm not worried about being overbuilt. Far from that.

insights.claim: Greenlight once calculated that meeting emissions-reduction goals requires approving about 600 large-scale clean energy projects per year, almost two per day.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Required throughput dwarfs current local approval capacity, so permitting remains a long-term bottleneck.
insights.quote: it was 600 projects per year. So almost two per day of these large scale clean energy projects

themes.theme: Local permitting as the binding constraint

insights.claim: The main obstacle to building clean power is neither technology nor cost but local permitting, where small, noisy opposition groups show up and supporters don't, so projects lose by forfeit.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Permitting/siting risk, not tech cost, is the key execution risk for renewable developers.
insights.quote: the big obstacle to doing that was not the technology which is well established or the cost. This was the cheapest and fastest energy to build. It was local permitting.

insights.claim: Counties are the most common decision-making body for clean energy siting, and there are more than 3,100 US counties, with municipalities deciding in some states, so there is no central repository of upcoming decisions.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Siting risk is extremely fragmented, rewarding whoever builds data infrastructure to track it.
insights.quote: There are more than 3,100 counties in the US and county is generally I'll get to this in a moment but county is the most common decision-making body

insights.claim: Most local ordinances Greenlight has seen advance are restrictive, ranging from outright bans to de facto bans via unreasonable setbacks.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Ordinances are a bigger threat than single-project denials since they foreclose future pipeline in a jurisdiction.
insights.quote: The majority of places that we've seen ordinances go forward, they are restrictive, right?

insights.claim: Some of the toughest siting territory is in blue places; New York State has many local battery storage bans and Santa Fe County was a hard fight, even as New York approved the Propel transmission line.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Do not assume progressive jurisdictions are easy siting markets; storage bans in NY are a specific headwind.
insights.quote: But there are a ton of places with bans on battery storage in New York State

insights.claim: Proposals to meet clean energy needs only with sites like parking-lot solar are partly fantasy: projects use land that has other uses, so building enough requires accepting trade-offs.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Utility-scale land-intensive projects remain necessary; distributed-only strategies won't close the gap.
insights.quote: These projects take up space. They use land. Most of the time, land is useful for something else to someone, right?

insights.claim: On state permitting reform, Illinois's law works well because it keeps decisions local but sets clear rules of the road, and any uncertainty in process gets exploited by opponents to derail projects.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: States with clear, certain siting criteria (e.g., Illinois) should carry lower permitting risk for developers.
insights.quote: if there's not certainty about the way the process works or what's able to be considered, then opponents will absolutely use whatever uncertainty there is to derail stuff

insights.claim: Project delays can cause cancellations or make equipment more expensive, rendering projects unviable, which is why speed should be a priority in permitting reform.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Permitting duration directly erodes project economics, not just timelines.

themes.theme: Greenlight's model, scale and win rates

insights.claim: Greenlight America runs an early warning system combining developer information-sharing (it is philanthropically, not developer, funded) with web scrapers and algorithmic review of thousands of local agenda and media alerts, plus a research team.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Systematic tracking of local hearings is an emerging data asset that could matter for siting-risk assessment.
insights.quote: we have web scrapers that gather this information we have algorithmic review to determine which of the alerts coming from these things

insights.claim: Greenlight says it has helped advance 67 GW of clean power across the US, which it equates to more than 1 billion tons of lifetime emissions averted and 3.5 times what it would take to power New York City (the host's intro cites 20.9 GW in 2025 and about 55.7 GW since the prior conversation).
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: A meaningful share of the US utility-scale pipeline now passes through organized local-support campaigns.
insights.quote: I'm pleased to share that we've now advanced 67 gawatts of clean power across the US.

insights.claim: Greenlight's win rate rose from 60% in its pilot to 75% last year and 79% so far this year, versus an industry baseline Traldy guesses is roughly a coin flip.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Organized supporter mobilization measurably raises approval odds for contested projects.
insights.quote: Last year, our win rate was 75%. this year so far it's 79%.

insights.claim: Using its scraping tools on historical decisions, Greenlight's early counterfactual analysis in the first several states found its win rate significantly above baseline.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Preliminary evidence that advocacy causally improves outcomes, though methodology is not detailed.

insights.claim: Greenlight went from four local wins in a quarter last year to eight local wins in a single day this month, reflecting the explosion of projects moving through permitting.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Hearing volume is spiking now, consistent with the deadline-driven sprint.
insights.quote: We had a day earlier this month where we had eight local winds in one day.

insights.claim: Greenlight has nearly 90 staff (fully remote, largest team is campaigns), raised almost $20 million this year, aims to raise more next year, and has worked with almost 300 local partner organizations.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Pro-build local advocacy is scaling quickly as a philanthropically funded field.
insights.quote: we've raised almost $20 million this year. We're looking to raise even more next year.

insights.claim: Neither Greenlight nor the field as a whole is close to covering 100% of local clean energy decisions, so there is substantial room and need to grow.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Most local siting decisions still go uncontested by supporters, leaving outcomes to opponents.

insights.claim: Greenlight is technology neutral but follows mass deployment, so its work is mostly solar, storage and wind with growing transmission work; it has not yet worked on geothermal and does not work for or against data centers.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Transmission siting is an expanding front for local mobilization.

insights.claim: Local decision makers are not deciding whether climate change is real but whether a project benefits the community, so effective messages center on economic benefits (big taxpayers funding public services) and property rights.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Local tax base and landowner-rights framing, not climate, drive approvals in conservative areas.
insights.quote: They're deciding should we build this project here? And that's about whether it will benefit the community.

insights.claim: A midsize utility-scale solar project roughly equals planting four million trees in emissions terms, and five local volunteers speaking at a county meeting can make the difference.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Tiny turnout can swing large-capacity decisions, an extremely high-leverage intervention.
insights.quote: a midsize utility scale solar project is roughly the equivalent of planting four million trees in terms of emissions

insights.claim: The feeling in the room drives what seems politically possible: if the first five speakers support a project it seems to sail through, if they oppose it, approval feels like political suicide, regardless of decision makers' priors.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Hearing dynamics, not community-wide opinion polls, determine approvals.
insights.quote: If the first five people speak up in favor of something, it feels like it's sailing through.

insights.claim: Local permitting decisions are not 50%-plus-one popularity contests but hinge on who shows up, so Greenlight focuses on supporters rather than trying to convert opponents.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Broad public polling on renewables is a poor predictor of local siting outcomes.
insights.quote: They're not a 50% plus one vote in the community. They're not a popularity contest.

insights.claim: Greenlight learned 'there is no bag': projects developers thought were safe lost when last-minute opposition appeared, so it now right-sizes by having supporters attend even when they may not need to speak.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Unopposed projects still carry late-stage siting risk; low-visibility strategies can backfire.
insights.quote: There is no bag. There's no such thing as being in the bag. It's not in the bag until you've won the vote.

insights.claim: Greenlight never shows up under its own name; it works through credible local partners across the spectrum, such as Faith in Place in Illinois, the conservative Land and Liberty, labor unions and Latinx groups.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Local credibility, not national advocacy brands, moves conservative local boards.
insights.quote: We're never showing up as Greenlight.

insights.claim: Most siting decisions occur in conservative areas made by conservative decision makers, who typically judge on local benefit or neighbor sentiment rather than national partisan cues about windmills.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Red-state siting risk is more local and negotiable than national rhetoric suggests.

insights.claim: Cited wins include a big solar project in Coles County, Illinois with Faith in Place; a Yakima County, Washington solar and agrivoltaics ordinance that became more permissive at the end after 10+ volunteers and 100+ petitions; and a rapid-response campaign for a 600 MW solar project in Morgan County, Colorado.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Concrete examples of contested utility-scale solar jurisdictions where organized support tipped outcomes.

insights.claim: Brokering talks between developers and groups with reasonable concerns can turn opposition into assets, e.g., introducing a reclaimed-mine-land solar developer to the local watershed association over watershed concerns.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Early stakeholder engagement on site-specific issues de-risks approvals.

insights.claim: When countering disinformation, Traldy recommends George Lakoff's truth sandwich (start with a shared value, name that disinformation exists without repeating it, redirect) and says showing up in person beats social media.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Repeating myths to debunk them spreads them; in-person constituent presence matters most to local officials.
insights.quote: you don't want to like repeat and then mythbust the disinformation. That just spreads it further.

insights.claim: Roberts worries that public fury at data centers (associated with AI, oligarchs and broad social ills) will spill over into opposition to electrification broadly, tainting solar, transmission and batteries.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Data center backlash is a cross-sector siting risk for renewables and grid infrastructure.

insights.claim: Greenlight is already seeing on campaigns that potential clean energy supporters are flipping to opposition or staying home because of a perceived link between clean energy and data centers, which Traldy calls more damaging than opponents exploiting the issue.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Data-center-linked load growth may raise local approval risk for nearby renewable projects.
insights.quote: many potential clean energy supporters, natural allies if you will, are either flipping to opposition or staying on the sidelines because of a perceived connection

insights.claim: Clean energy opponents sometimes exploit grassroots data center opposition by trumping up connections to clean energy projects, and Roberts claims Steve Bannon is doing this deliberately.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Organized political actors are bundling AI backlash with renewables opposition.

insights.claim: A common misconception is that blocking a local solar project will keep a rumored data center away; Traldy doubts tech companies would forgo a data center because a solar project wasn't built.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Blocking renewables likely doesn't stop data centers, it just changes their power mix.

insights.claim: Traldy expects the data center-clean energy confusion can never be fully eliminated, only managed and chipped away at campaign by campaign, though some communities that already approved a data center want clean energy to supply it.
insights.speaker: Matt Traldy (CEO, Greenlight America)
insights.so_what: Treat data center spillover as a persistent background risk factor in siting rather than a solvable problem.
